newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spanish markets penalised by EMU delays worries.
newsitem.headline: Spanish markets penalised by EMU delays worries.

text.p: Spanish financial markets were punished on Monday as dealers adopted a more cautious stance toward Spain's chances of being in Europe's single currency from the outset.

Although a correction was long overdue after peseta markets soared amid views Spain would join in the launch, analysts said sentiment had changed after German remarks suggesting Spanish participation might destabilise the project.
"This could be the news this week -- a more cautious approach toward EMU," said Valentin Fernandez, economist at Credit Lyonnais in Madrid.
He stressed that in the latest Spanish-German summit "Kohl's remarks seemed very diplomatic and cool."

This morning, a senior Dresdner Bank AG executive said he was very concerned the debate about whether Italy and Spain would be among the economic and monetary union's (EMU) first participants was unsettling financial markets.
His comments followed remarks over the weekend by other German bankers who held out the prospect of turmoil on financial markets if countries like Italy joined from the start.
The peseta, Spanish bonds and shares all fell as markets realised that what had appeared within the nation's grasp might be more difficult to achieve than they had imagined.
The peseta traded on Monday at its lowest levels since August at around 84.90 per mark, a bit lower than late Friday's 84.65/68 but far from its low of 83.30 hit mid January.
The Bank of Spain, which had been selling pesetas to smooth the currency's climb, turned around last Thursday and starting buying them, dealers added.
To dealers, the peseta's weakness was a sign foreigners were exporting their Iberian investments back to core countries.
Madrid stocks lost ground, with the blue chip index (IBEX-35) near 5,304, a 0.43-percent decline from Friday. That compares with an all-time high at 5,571 in mid-January.

"This correction is mainly due to German comments and to the fact the market realised that the Bank of Spain's room for further reductions in rates is not that much," said Luis Alzola, economist at Salomon Brothers in London.
European officials said they would decide by the end of February whether to consider Italy's Euro tax a one-off measure or a real reduction in the 1997 deficit.
Spanish markets are concerned that if Italy is left out of EMU at its start, Spain will also find itself ou on the street.
"(Still) if this is the case and Spain should enter one or two years later, long-term bond prices should not lose more than 15/20 basis points," Alzola said.

The 10-year Spanish yield spread versus Bunds, considered a measure of market confidence in Spain's entry to EMU, traded back above 100 basis points on Monday, a level broken to the downside in mid-January in a steady decline that started in March 1996.
In March, the spread was around 330 basis points and near 500 basis points during summer, 1995.
But some traders said the move back up above 100 basis points could be a simple correction.
"At the beginning of this year, our forecast was for the 10-year spread to be around 75 basis points by December...It was almost there already," Alzola said.
The spread hit a record low 84 basis points on January 22.
The yield curve change was even more pronounced, flattening as expectations of sharp declines in the key money market rate were falling apart, dealers said.
